claims.text: Above 900 °C, oxide-layer formation and persistence in CrFeCoNiX alloys are governed by interactions between each alloying element and the oxidative or corrosive environment.
Thermodynamics governs the element-environment interactions that determine oxide formation and stability.
In-situ atom probe tomography and transmission electron microscopy can predict and optimize protective-oxide behavior by resolving oxidation mechanisms and oxide-structure evolution.
Changing the concentration of Si, Mn, or Al in CrFeCoNiX alters the surface oxide layer's composition and structure.
Surface oxide composition and structure mediate whether the oxide remains protective or cracks and spalls.
Depending on composition and exposure conditions, CrFeCoNiX may form either a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide or an oxide that cracks and spalls.
CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY systems contain known examples of stable and unstable oxide-forming alloys.
The proposed behavior applies to single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
The proposed behavior applies during prolonged exposure above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
The exact physical causes of oxide cracking and spallation are unresolved.
The optimal composition and exposure conditions for producing a stable protective oxide are unknown.
Oxide thickness, composition, morphology, roughness, elemental distribution, and segregation are measurable indicators of oxide behavior.
Formation of an unstable oxide despite a supposedly stabilizing element or condition would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome already permits cracking and spallation depending on unspecified composition and exposure conditions, while the falsification rule treats the same observation as falsifying under an undefined 'supposedly stabilizing' condition. No composition or condition is prospectively designated as stabilizing, so the rule does not cleanly contradict the hypothesis's allowed outcomes.
